summary: "Instead of fine-tuning a model to ignore injected instructions, this defense learns a handful of per-head attention gates that keep untrusted tokens in their lane — and holds up against adaptive white-box attacks."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-10-29-heads-of-security-attention-gates.svg"

Most prompt injection defenses work by fine-tuning: teach the model to distinguish instructions from data, and hope the separation holds. **Heads of Security (HoS)** attacks the problem one layer lower — it learns a small set of **per-head attention gates** that control how each attention head redistributes mass between trusted and untrusted tokens, enforcing instruction–data separation without touching the model's weights.

The authors (Igor Shilov, Xiaoxue Yang, Alexander Panfilov, Evgenii Kortukov, Matthieu Meeus, Peter Romov and colleagues) evaluate on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B against two comparators: **SecAlign++**, a state-of-the-art fine-tuning-based defense, and **ASIDE**, an architectural defense that also builds instruction–data separation into the model.

## The attack numbers

The black-box **RL-Hammer** attack reaches a **97% attack success rate against GPT-OSS-20B** and **85% against SecAlign** — but only **10% against HoS**. The white-box **Claudini** attack, which was specifically strengthened against HoS through automated adversarial research, needs **three times more FLOPs** to reach the same success rate on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign.

Utility tells the same story. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, while SecAlign and ASIDE both **degrade in few-shot settings**. On agentic benchmarks under static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security–utility trade-off over the base model — but **ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility**, despite being the other architecture-level approach in the comparison.

The pattern worth noting: among the two defenses that bake separation into the architecture, one of them trades away the ability to use tools at all. That is a strong argument that architectural defenses need to be evaluated on agentic workloads, not just on classification-style benchmarks where utility degradation hides.

The paper is on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37657) under ID 2610.37657, submitted 27 October 2026.
